To check if an item exists, hash it with the same $K$ functions: if any bit is 0, the item is definitely NOT in the set. If all bits are 1, the item MIGHT be in the set.

guarantees.falsePositives: Possible (Can say 'Yes' when an item isn't there due to hash bit collisions).
guarantees.falseNegatives: Impossible (Will NEVER say 'No' if the item was added).

techUseCases: Preventing Cache Penetration: Checking if a user ID exists before hitting the database.
Cassandra & RocksDB SSTables: Checking if a key exists in an on-disk SSTable to avoid wasted disk seeks.
Web Crawlers: Checking if a URL has already been scraped.

structures.name: HyperLogLog (HLL)
structures.purpose: Estimating cardinality (count of unique items) in massive data streams using almost zero memory.
structures.theProblem: Counting unique visitors across 100 million users with a `Set` or SQL `COUNT(DISTINCT)` requires Gigabytes of RAM storing all raw user IDs.
structures.howItWorks: Hashes incoming values and inspects the number of leading zeros in the binary hash output. A sequence of 10 leading zeros has a probability of 1 in $2^{10}$ (1,024). By averaging observations across thousands of internal registers, it estimates unique items within a ~1% error margin.
structures.memoryEfficiency: Can count billions of unique elements with less than 1.5 KB of fixed memory.
techUseCases: Reddit/Twitter unique daily view counts on viral posts.

structures.name: Trie (Prefix Tree)
structures.purpose: Fast prefix-based string searching, dictionary lookup, and real-time autocomplete suggestions.
structures.howItWorks: A tree where each node represents a character. All descendants of a node share a common string prefix. Nodes can store popular search frequency weights.
structures.complexity: Lookup time is $O(L)$, where $L$ is the length of the search word, completely independent of the total millions of words stored in the dictionary.
techUseCases: Google search bar autocomplete suggestions ("sys..." -> "system design").
Spell checkers and predictive text algorithms.

topics.title: Data Warehouse vs Data Lake
topics.summary: High-volume analytical data architectures designed for reporting, business intelligence (BI), and machine learning.
topics.simpleDefinition: A Data Warehouse is a cleaned, highly-structured grocery store shelf; a Data Lake is a vast, natural reservoir where water flows in completely raw.

dataWarehouse.paradigm: Schema-on-Write (Data must be cleaned, transformed, and structured before loading).
dataWarehouse.dataTypes: Cleaned, structured relational data from transactional OLTP databases.
dataWarehouse.storageFormat: Columnar storage (e.g., Parquet, internal proprietary block formats) to optimize aggregations (`SUM`, `AVG`).
dataWarehouse.primaryUsers: Business Analysts, Product Managers, BI dashboard tools (Tableau, Metabase).

dataLake.paradigm: Schema-on-Read (Dump raw data first; parse structure only when querying).
dataLake.dataTypes: Raw, unstructured, semi-structured data (JSON logs, sensor telemetry, audio files, raw CSVs).
dataLake.storageFormat: Low-cost cloud object storage buckets (S3 / GCS / Azure ADLS) organized by dates.
dataLake.primaryUsers: Data Scientists, Machine Learning Engineers building AI models, Big Data engineers.

topics.title: Processing Paradigms: Batch vs Stream (Spark vs Flink)
topics.summary: Analyzing historical data in periodic chunks versus processing live data points continuously in real time.

paradigms.concept: Collects data over a period (e.g., 24 hours), stores it, and runs heavy distributed compute jobs overnight.

characteristics.dataBound: Bounded datasets with a clear beginning and end.
characteristics.computeModel: High throughput over large historical datasets.

paradigms.techExample: Calculating monthly employee payroll, generating quarterly financial compliance tax reports.

paradigms.concept: Processes each individual event or micro-batch continuously as it arrives over a live message pipe.

characteristics.dataBound: Unbounded streams that never stop emitting data.
characteristics.computeModel: Event-by-event stateful processing using tumbling, sliding, or session time windows.

paradigms.leadTechnology: Apache Flink (True low-latency event-driven stream processing)
paradigms.techExample: Live credit card fraud detection (freezing a transaction within 50ms if geo-location jumps unrealistically), real-time ride pricing surges in Uber.

topics.architectTakeaway: Modern architectures often combine both into a Lambda Architecture (Batch layer for historical accuracy + Speed layer for real-time views) or a Kappa Architecture (all data processed as a single continuous real-time stream using Kafka + Flink).

description: Essential identity, cryptography, traffic protection, and defense patterns required to protect distributed production systems from breach and resource exhaustion.

topics.title: AuthN vs AuthZ (Authentication vs Authorization)
topics.summary: The fundamental distinction between verifying someone's identity versus enforcing their access privileges.
topics.simpleDefinition: Authentication verifies WHO you are; Authorization determines WHAT you are allowed to do.
topics.everydayAnalogy: Your passport proves your citizenship and identity at the airport gate (Authentication). Your boarding pass dictates whether you can sit in Business Class or Economy (Authorization).

authentication.failureResponse: HTTP 401 Unauthorized (Identity could not be confirmed or credentials missing)
authentication.techExample: Logging into GitHub using your username, password, and Hardware YubiKey OTP.

authorization.coreQuestion: "Do you have permission to access or modify this specific resource?"
authorization.failureResponse: HTTP 403 Forbidden (We know who you are, but you lack permission to perform this action)
authorization.techExample: A junior engineer trying to click 'Delete Production Database' on AWS console is blocked because their IAM policy only grants Read-Only access.

topics.title: OAuth 2.0 & OpenID Connect (OIDC)
topics.summary: The modern standard protocol for delegated authorization and federated identity without password sharing.
topics.simpleDefinition: OAuth 2.0 lets you give a third-party app limited permission to access your data on another service without giving them your master password.
topics.everydayAnalogy: A valet key for your car: It lets the parking attendant start the engine and drive 100 meters, but cannot open the locked glove compartment or the trunk.

coreActors.name: Resource Owner
coreActors.role: The end user who owns the account/data.

coreActors.name: Client
coreActors.role: The third-party application trying to access user resources (e.g., Spotify website).

coreActors.name: Authorization Server
coreActors.role: The trusted identity provider holding the master credentials (e.g., Google Accounts, GitHub Auth).

coreActors.name: Resource Server
coreActors.role: The API hosting the protected user data (e.g., Google Calendar API, GitHub Repos API).

authorizationCodeGrantFlow: 1. User clicks 'Sign in with Google' on third-party website.
2. Client redirects user to Google's consent screen requesting specific scopes (`email`, `calendar.readonly`).
3. User approves; Google redirects user back to Client's callback URL with a short-lived one-time `Authorization Code`.
4. Client's backend server sends this Code directly to Google's token endpoint over a secure backchannel (along with `Client Secret` / PKCE code verifier).
5. Google verifies and exchanges the Code for an `Access Token` (and optionally a `Refresh Token` and `ID Token`).
6. Client uses the Access Token in the HTTP Authorization header (`Bearer <token>`) to fetch data from the Resource Server.
topics.oidcDistinction: OAuth 2.0 is purely for Authorization (gives access tokens). OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that introduces the `ID Token` (a signed JWT) to handle Authentication.

topics.title: Stateful Sessions vs Stateless JWTs
topics.summary: Comparing traditional server-side session cookies against cryptographically signed token-based authorization.

comparisonTable.sessionBased: Stateful: Server generates an opaque random session ID stored in a centralized cache (Redis) or database. Client keeps it in an `HttpOnly` cookie.
comparisonTable.jwtBased: Stateless: All user identity and claims (role, email, user_id) are encoded directly inside the signed token payload kept on the client.

comparisonTable.sessionBased: Requires looking up Redis on every single request across all microservices to check session validity.
comparisonTable.jwtBased: Microservices verify the token locally in microseconds using the shared secret or public RSA/ECDSA key without calling a centralized auth DB.

comparisonTable.sessionBased: Instant and trivial: Simply delete the session ID key from Redis.
comparisonTable.jwtBased: Extremely difficult: Once issued, a JWT remains valid until its expiration time unless you maintain a distributed token blacklist (which reintroduces state).

comparisonTable.sessionBased: Tiny: Only passes a 32-character random string in the cookie header.
comparisonTable.jwtBased: Larger: Includes header, payload, and cryptographic signature (often 500+ bytes sent on every HTTP request).

topics.productionBestPractice: Use short-lived Access Tokens (e.g., JWT valid for 15 minutes) paired with long-lived, revocable Refresh Tokens (stored statefully in Redis and sent via secure `HttpOnly` cookies).

topics.title: Encryption: In Transit vs At Rest
topics.summary: Protecting data while moving across public cables and while permanently resting on disk drives.
topics.simpleDefinition: In Transit protects data from wiretapping as it travels across the internet; At Rest protects data if someone physically steals the hard drive or backup snapshot.

breakdown.threatProtected: Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) snooping, packet sniffing at ISP/public Wi-Fi level.
breakdown.howItWorks: Encrypted using TLS 1.3 (Transport Layer Security). Begins with an asymmetric handshake (RSA/Diffie-Hellman) to authenticate server identity, then shifts to fast symmetric encryption (AES-256-GCM / ChaCha20) for session data.
techImplementations: mTLS (Mutual TLS): Both client and server present certificates to authenticate each other (standard inside Kubernetes service meshes like Istio).

breakdown.threatProtected: Physical server theft from datacenters, compromised cloud volume snapshots, unauthenticated disk reads.
breakdown.howItWorks: Data is encrypted right before being written to physical disk sectors using symmetric algorithms (AES-256).
techImplementations: Hardware/OS level: AWS KMS (Key Management Service) integrating with EBS volume encryption and S3 bucket default encryption.

Application level (Envelope Encryption): Encrypt sensitive columns (e.g., credit card numbers, tax IDs) using a Data Encryption Key (DEK), which is itself encrypted by a Master Key (KEK) stored inside a Hardware Security Module (HSM).

topics.title: DDoS Attacks & Multi-Layer Defense
topics.summary: Techniques for shielding system availability against massive malicious flood traffic.
topics.simpleDefinition: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attempts to crash an application by overwhelming its network bandwidth, socket connections, or CPU with bot traffic from thousands of infected machines.

attackTypes: SYN Flood (exhausting half-open TCP connection tables)
defenseStrategy: Anycast DNS routing: Spreads attack volume geographically across hundreds of edge data centers worldwide so no single pipe gets saturated.
Edge scrubbing centers (Cloudflare, AWS Shield Advanced) that drop malformed TCP/UDP packets at line rate before reaching origin infrastructure.

attackTypes: HTTP Flood (hammering expensive database search endpoints with millions of `GET /search?q=...` calls)
Slowloris (opening thousands of HTTP connections and sending headers excruciatingly slowly to starve server thread pools)
defenseStrategy: Web Application Firewall (WAF): Inspects request patterns, user-agent fingerprints, and blocks known bot signatures.
Managed CAPTCHA challenges (Cloudflare Turnstile) triggered on anomalous traffic surges.
Granular Rate Limiting at the API Gateway: Throttles requests by IP address, API key, or JWT sub-claim.

rateLimitingDefenseIntegration.placement: Terminate and rate-limit as close to the edge as possible (CDN/Cloudflare) so origin backend CPU and database connection pools are never spent parsing malicious payloads.
rateLimitingDefenseIntegration.statusCodes: Return `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests` accompanied by `Retry-After: <seconds>` headers.

module: Low Level Design (LLD) & Object-Oriented Software Architecture
description: Clean code architecture, object-oriented design principles, behavioral/creational patterns, and step-by-step entity modeling for classic machine-coding interview problems.

sections.summary: Five foundational object-oriented design guidelines that prevent tight coupling, code rot, and brittle software.

principles.name: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
principles.simpleDefinition: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.
principles.everydayAnalogy: A Swiss Army Knife is handy, but in a professional kitchen, a chef uses a dedicated knife for cutting and a separate bottle opener for drinks. Don't build all-in-one God classes.
principles.codeSmell: An `Invoice` class that calculates total prices, saves invoice rows to PostgreSQL, and sends the PDF via SendGrid email.
principles.correctDesign: Split into three classes: `InvoiceCalculator` (business math), `InvoiceRepository` (database persistence), and `InvoiceNotificationService` (email delivery).
principles.interviewImpact: Interviewers look for this first when checking whether your domain entities are doing presentation or storage work.

principles.name: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
principles.simpleDefinition: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.
principles.everydayAnalogy: Your smartphone has an extension slot (app store/plugins). You don't open the motherboard and re-solder chips every time you want a new photo filter.
principles.codeSmell: A payment service containing `if (type == 'CREDIT_CARD') ... else if (type == 'UPI') ... else if (type == 'CRYPTO')`. Adding a new payment method modifies core tested code.
principles.correctDesign: Define a `PaymentProcessor` interface with a `processPayment(amount)` method. Implement `UpiPaymentProcessor`, `CreditCardProcessor`, and inject via Polymorphism.
principles.interviewImpact: Demonstrates that adding a new business feature will never introduce regression bugs in existing, production-tested features.

principles.name: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
principles.simpleDefinition: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.
principles.everydayAnalogy: If it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck but needs batteries, you probably have the wrong abstraction.
principles.codeSmell: Class `Square` inherits from `Rectangle`. Changing `setWidth(w)` on a Square forces its height to change implicitly, violating caller expectations for a Rectangle.
principles.correctDesign: Create a shared interface `Shape` with `calculateArea()`, rather than forcing inappropriate inheritance between Square and Rectangle.
principles.interviewImpact: Prevents throwing unexpected `UnsupportedOperationException` or silent state corruption in subclasses.

principles.name: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
principles.simpleDefinition: Clients should never be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
principles.everydayAnalogy: A restaurant menu with 500 items where you are forced to order a drink, dessert, and steak even if you only wanted a coffee.
principles.codeSmell: A monolithic interface `Worker` with methods `work()`, `eat()`, and `sleep()`. When implementing `RobotWorker`, you are forced to provide dummy empty implementations for `eat()` and `sleep()`.
principles.correctDesign: Decompose into lean interfaces: `Workable`, `Feedable`, `Sleepable`. `Human` implements all three, while `Robot` implements only `Workable`.
principles.interviewImpact: Keeps interfaces small, cohesive, and decoupled.

principles.name: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
principles.simpleDefinition: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.
principles.everydayAnalogy: You plug a lamp into a standard wall socket (interface). You don't solder lamp wires directly into the municipal electrical grid wires (concrete implementation).
principles.codeSmell: A `NotificationService` directly instantiating `new TwilioSmsClient()` inside its constructor. Swapping to AWS SNS requires rewriting the service.
principles.correctDesign: High-level `NotificationService` depends on an abstraction `MessageSender`. `TwilioSmsClient` implements `MessageSender` and is injected via constructor injection.
principles.interviewImpact: Enables seamless unit testing with mocks and stubs.

sections.summary: Proven object-oriented blueprints to solve recurring code structure and behavioral problems.

patterns.name: Singleton Pattern
patterns.intent: Ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global point of access to it.
patterns.realWorldTechUse: Database connection pools, Hardware logger instances, Runtime configuration loaders.
patterns.implementationWatchouts: Use double-checked locking with a `volatile` keyword in Java/C++ to prevent race conditions during lazy initialization; beware that singletons make unit testing hard if overused.

patterns.name: Factory / Abstract Factory Pattern
patterns.intent: Define an interface for creating objects without specifying the exact concrete class to instantiate.
patterns.realWorldTechUse: Cross-platform UI renderers (ButtonFactory producing MacButton or WindowsButton), dynamic notification generators (SMSFactory vs EmailFactory).
patterns.implementationWatchouts: Avoid writing huge switch statements inside one class; pair it with a registration map for dynamic runtime discovery.
interviewChecklist: Factory class/method determining instance creation based on inputs

patterns.name: Observer Pattern
patterns.intent: Define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.
patterns.realWorldTechUse: Pub-Sub event dispatchers, frontend state management (Redux/MobX), Spring ApplicationEvent listeners, stock market ticker subscriber displays.
patterns.implementationWatchouts: Memory leaks in long-running applications (dangling listeners that forget to unsubscribe); thread safety when iterating subscriber lists.

patterns.name: Strategy Pattern
patterns.intent: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable at runtime.
patterns.realWorldTechUse: Dynamic payment processing (CreditCard vs PayPal vs UPI), surge pricing algorithms in Uber, route planners in Google Maps (Fastest vs Shortest vs Toll-Free).
patterns.implementationWatchouts: Client must be aware of the different strategies to inject the correct one, or a factory should choose it based on payload metadata.
interviewChecklist: Strategy interface declaring common algorithm method
Context class holding a strategy reference

patterns.name: Decorator Pattern
patterns.intent: Attach additional responsibilities and behavior to an object dynamically without modifying original class code or using inheritance explosion.
patterns.realWorldTechUse: Java I/O streams (`new BufferedReader(new FileReader(file)))`, coffee shop billing customizations (BaseCoffee + MilkDecorator + WhipCreamDecorator), HTTP request middleware chains.
patterns.implementationWatchouts: Can create lots of tiny objects that make debugging stack traces confusing if nested too deep.
interviewChecklist: Abstract decorator implementing base interface and holding a base component reference

sections.summary: Deep architectural walkthroughs of the 5 most frequently asked LLD problems in Tier-1 tech interviews.

problems.title: Design a Parking Lot System
problems.problemScope: Multi-floor parking lot supporting different vehicle types (Motorbike, Car, Truck), spot allocations, ticket issuance, and automated billing strategies.

coreEntities.name: ParkingLot
coreEntities.responsibility: Singleton controller managing floors, entrance gates, and exit gates.

coreEntities.name: ParkingFloor
coreEntities.responsibility: Contains a collection of numbered parking spots and live availability boards.

coreEntities.name: ParkingSpot
coreEntities.responsibility: Abstract class with subtypes (CompactSpot, LargeSpot, HandicappedSpot, BikeSpot). Holds spot status and occupied vehicle pointer.

coreEntities.name: Vehicle
coreEntities.responsibility: Abstract base class with license plate and `VehicleType` enum.

coreEntities.name: Ticket
coreEntities.responsibility: Holds unique ticket ID, entry timestamp, assigned spot ID, and vehicle details.

coreEntities.name: EntranceGate / ExitGate
coreEntities.responsibility: Handles barrier physical operations, scanning, and ticket printing.

patternsUsed: Factory Pattern: For spot allocation strategy based on `VehicleType`.
Strategy Pattern: For dynamic fee calculation (e.g., HourlyFeeStrategy vs FlatDayRateStrategy vs PeakHourRateStrategy).
concurrencyAndEdgeCases: Race conditions: Two cars arriving at two different entrance gates simultaneously trying to claim the last available spot. Fix with row-level database locking or thread-safe atomic sets (`ConcurrentSkipListSet`).
Handling oversized vehicles taking multiple spots.

problems.title: Design an LRU Cache (In-Memory)
problems.problemScope: Fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used element in strict O(1) time complexity for both get and put operations.

coreEntities.name: Node
coreEntities.responsibility: Doubly linked list element containing key, value, prev pointer, and next pointer.

coreEntities.name: DoublyLinkedList
coreEntities.responsibility: Maintains head (most recent) and tail (least recent). Implements `addFirst(Node)`, `removeNode(Node)`, and `moveToHead(Node)` in O(1).

coreEntities.name: LRUCache
coreEntities.responsibility: Holds max capacity, current size, and a Hash Map mapping `Key -> Node`.

patternsUsed: Composition: Combining a HashMap with an internal Doubly Linked List.
keyAPIs: `get(K key): V` - If found, move node to head and return value. If not found, return null or -1.
`put(K key, V value): void` - If key exists, update value and move to head. If new, create node, add to head; if capacity exceeded, remove tail node and delete from hash map.
concurrencyAndEdgeCases: Thread safety: Making read/write operations non-blocking across multiple threads. Use `ReadWriteLock` (allowing multiple readers or one writer) or segment-level striped locking rather than a slow global synchronized block.
Handling keys with TTL expiration alongside LRU ordering.

Floating-point rounding errors: Handling fractional pennies (e.g., $100 split 3 ways yields 33.33 + 33.33 + 33.34).
